OBSERVANCE OF SILENCE IN MEMORY OF THE FATHER 
OF THE NATION AND OTHERS WHO GAVE THEIR LIVES 
IN THE STRUGGLE FOR INDIA'S FREEDOM 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, today is 30 th January, the 
Martyrdom Day of Mahatma Gandhi, the Father of the Nation. Before we 
take up today's agenda, I request Member s to rise in their places and observe 
silence for two minutes in his memory and all those who gave their lives in 
the struggle for India's freedom. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to 
the passing away of Shrimati Pratibha Singh and Shri Ramakrishna Hegde, 
former Members of this House. 
Shrimati Pratibha Singh passed away on 8th January, 2004 at the age 
of 75 years. 
Born at Salemgarh, District Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, in July, 1929, 
Shrimati Singh had her education at Women's College, Patna. 
An active social and political wo rker, Shrimati Singh took keen 
interest in the uplift of Harijans and welfare of women and children. She was 
also associated with various social  and welfare organisations and was 
instrumental in the establishment of  "Saket Home for Handicapped" in 
Chandigarh. She started the scheme fo r Indian Holiday Home at Taradevi 
near Shimla.   She was President of the Child Welfare Council, Punjab and 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [30 January, 2004] 
Red Cross Society, Punjab, from 1953 to 1958. She attended the Inter-
Parliamentary Conference at Berlin in the year 1986  and was Member of the 
Indian delegation to the United Nations in 1982. 
Shrimati Pratibha Singh represented the State of Bihar in this House 
for four consecutive terms from Decembe r, 1970 to April, 1976; from April, 
1976 to April, 1982; from April, 1982 to April, 1988 and again from April, 
1988 to July, 1992. 
In the passing away of Shrimati Pratibha Singh, the country has lost 
a distinguished social worker and a noted Parliamentarian. Shri Ramakrishna 
Hegde passed away on the 12th January, 2004 at the age of 78 years following 
brain haemorrhage. 
Born at Siddapur, District North Kanara, Karnataka in August, 1926, 
Shri Hegde had his education at SIRSI, Kashi Vidyapeeth, Banaras and the 
Lucknow University. 
A lawyer by profession,  Shri  Hedge plunged himself into the 
freedom struggle and was jailed during the 'Quit India Movement' in 1942. He  
took  keen  interest  in  the  fields  of photography,  acting  in  movies, 
literature, fine arts and music. 
Suave and soft-spoken, Shri Hegde had a long and distinguished 
political career. He started his political  career with the Membership of the 
Karnataka Legislative Asse mbly in the year 1957 and was again elected to 
that Assembly in the years 1962, 1967, 1983, 1985 and 1989. He was a 
Deputy Minister in the Government of  Karnataka in the year 1957 and was 
Cabinet Minister in the State Government between 1962 to 1971, holding 
portfolios of Youth, Welfare and Sports, Cooperation, Industries, Planning, 
Panchayati Raj, Development, Information and Publicity and Excise and 
Finance. He was a member of the Karnataka Legislative Council from 1972 to 
1978, and was the Leader of the Opposition during that period. Shri Hegde 
became the Chief Minister of Karnataka in the year 1983 and held the post till 
September, 1988. As Chief Minister, he introduced many welfare schemes for 
the benefit of the weaker sections of th e society, backward classes, Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes and minorities. Known for his 'value-based 
politics' he also established the institution of Lokayukta for the first time in 
India to enquire into charges of corruption against Ministers including the 
Chief Minister. 
Shri Hegde represented the State of Karnataka in this House for two 
terms from April, 1978 to May, 1983 and from April, 1996 to April, 2002. 
2 

[30 January, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
He also served as the Union Minister of Commerce from 1998 to 1999. She 
Hegde also had the distinction of serving as the Deputy Chairman of the 
Planning Commission of India from 1989 to 1990. 
Shri Hegde was General-Secretary of  the All India Janata Party for 
six years. He was also the Vice-Presid ent of the Janata Dal and the Founder 
President of the Lok Shakti Party. He had several publications on varied 
subjects to his credit. 
In the passing away of Shri Ramakrishna Hegde the country has lost 
a distinguished and dedicated political worker, an eminent Parliamentarian 
and an able administrator. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shrimati Pratibha Singh and 
Shri Ramakrishna Hegde. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence for one 
minute as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.)

REFERENCE TO VICTIMS OF EARTHQUAKE AT BAM IN IRAN 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members; the House expresses its heartfelt 
sympathies and condolences to the frien dly people of Iran on the suffering 
caused by the devastating earthquake which hit Bam on the 26 th December, 
2003. More than 35,000 people are feared dead while thousands of people are 
injured. Immense damage was caused to properties. 
This House notes that the Government of India has committed 10 
million US dollars towards relief assistance to the victims of the earthquake. 
The Government of India was quick to send a team of doctors which set up a 
field hospital at Bam complete with medicines, equipments and surgical 
facilities. Other relief materials such as blankets and high protein biscuits 
were also sent for the disaster relief. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the memory of those who lost their lives in this tragedy. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute)

MATTER RAISED WITH PERMISSION 
Extension of the Winter Session of Parliament after its adjournment sine die 
on 23rd December, 2003 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir, with 
your permission, I would like to draw the attention of the House and the 
Government to a matter which has been agitating our mind. 
Sir, the Winter Session of Parliament began on 2 nd December, after 
being summoned by the President of the Republic under article 85 clause (1). 
On 23rd December, the House was adjourned sine die by the hon. Chairman of 
the House. And we have been asked, un der your orders in Bulletin No. 4167, 
dated 21st January, to assemble on 30 th January. In between, we are hearing 
that the Lok Sabha is going to be di ssolved; Vote on Account is to be 
approved by the Lok Sabha; there will be  a premature termination of the Lok 
Sabha and the General Elections will take place.  I 
6 

[30 January, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
am unable to understand what prompted the Government to take this decision, 
keeping everybody in the dark. Gener al Election is not an unusual event. 
Premature termination of Lok Sabha is also not an unusual event. If I 
remember correctly, it happened in 1970;  it happened in 1977; it happened in 
1979. It has happened umpteen number of times; and, as per the 
parliamentary practice, it is the prerogat ive of the Prime Minister to decide it. 
He can recommend to the President the dissolution of the House and the 
President can dissolve the House, in ex ercise of the power conferred on him 
by the Constitution. But what is the rationale behind extending the Winter 
Session? Approval of the Vote on Accoun t because the full Budget cannot be 
placed before the House due to General El ection, is not an unusual thing. My 
colleague, Dr. Manmohan Singh, who is sitting on my right, had presented the 
Vote on Account in 1996. He did not present the full Budget. That was the 
election year. We have seen it on a numb er of occasions that the Vote on 
Account is approved by the Lok Sabh a normally in an election year, if the 
elections are held earlier. If I remember correctly, in 1971, the Vote on 
Account was approved by Lok Sabha on 27-28 th March. It had happened in 
1977. The new Government came into existence on 23 rd March and the Vote 
on Account was approved by the Lok Sabha. 
Now, the problem is that the Houses are adjourned sine die by the 
respective Presiding Officers. In regar d to the prorogation, which is a 
constitutional requirement, the Presidi ng Officers of both t he Houses have a 
role to play. My point is that the Government of the day, to fulfil its own political 
agenda, to serve its own political agenda, has used the offices of the Presiding 
Officers. What happens normally in the case of prorogation is that after the 
House is adjourned sine die - after a couple of days - the Secretaries-General 
of the respective Houses enquire from the Government, from the Minister of 
Parliamentary Affairs, as to when the Government is going to prorogue the 
House. The President cannot prorogue th e House on his own. He requires an 
advice from the Council of Ministers, fr om the Prime Minister, as far as the 
summoning, the prorogation or the dissol ution of the House is concerned. If 
the Government had decided to hold elections, to terminate Lok Sabha 
prematurely, even then the Houses could have been called after the 
prorogation in the month of  January, or in the month of February, and after 
taking the Vote on Account, the House could have been dissolved. Heavens 
would not have fallen. In this case, we are doing away with another 
constitutional requirement which is under  article 87, clause 1. As per that, the 
President is to address the Joint Session of both 
7

the Houses at the beginnin g of each year. Mr. Chairman, Sir, there is a little 
history behind it. Even the very first amendment of the Constitution in 1951 
took place on this issue. The original article 87 stipulated that each session of 
the Parliament was to be addressed by  the President. Therefore, after the 
adoption of the Constitution on 26 th January, 1950, when three sessions of the 
provisional Parliament took place,  every session was addressed by the 
President, and it was pointed out that it is inconvenient. So, the first 
amendment to the Constitution took pl ace in 1951 for amending article 87 and 
making a provision that the President will address only the first session of the 
year, and in an election year, as article 87 requires, the President is to address 
both the Houses after the new Lok Sabha is constituted. Therefore, the normal 
practice all these years is that in an election year, the President addresses 
both the Houses twice, once at the beginning of the year, when the first 
session takes place, and again when the new Lok Sabha is constituted. We 
understand that the Government wanted to hold the elections early and for that 
obvious reason it is the Executive's pr erogative, it is the Prime Minister's 
prerogative to do it. Everybody understands that. But, what is not 
understandable is, what would have happened if there was a normal session 
and if the President would have address ed it and if there was a debate on the 
Address of the President, which is the normal practice. Here the Members get 
the opportunity of reviewing the functi oning of the Government for the whole 
year which is contained in  the statement, in the Address of the Presidentl We 
are deprived of that opportunity. That st atement is not drafted by anybody else 
other than the Cabinet, and it speaks not hing else but the platitude of the 
Government. It may provide how India shines, how they feel good, and we 
have the opportunity to review the performance of the Government. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, especially in this year, it was required because the 
Winter Session was shortened. Since th is Government came to power, from 
1998 onwards, if you calculate the number of days of actual sittings, you will 
find that every time the days of Se ssions have been reduced. Those days are 
gone when Winter Sessions used to be for six weeks, Monsoon Sessions used 
to be for six weeks and Budget Sessions used to be for more than 12 weeks. 
This time also, we met in the Winter Session on 2 nd of December and we 
adjourned sine die on 23 rd December. We are deprived of having the 
opportunity of reviewing the performanc e of the Government which is being 
provided in the Address of the President, and the President is also deprived of 
addressing the two Houses of Parliament in the election

Houses would be prorogued, and only after ascertaining this fact the

Secretary-General of Rajya Sabha - send the communication to the Secretary
